subject: rla
title: Grammar II: Agreement, Pronouns, Tense, Confused Words, Capitals, Apostrophes, Commas
objectives: You will make verbs agree with their real subjects, including subjects separated from the verb by phrases, indefinite pronouns such as each and everyone, and subjects joined by and, or, and nor.
You will choose pronouns that agree with their antecedents and use the correct case (I or me, she or her, he or him, who or whom), even in pairs.
You will keep verb tense consistent by following time clues, and use has or have with the correct past participle.
You will tell frequently confused words apart (its/it's, their/there/they're, your/you're, affect/effect, than/then) and apply the rules for capital letters, apostrophes, and commas.
You will answer GED-style drop-down editing items by spotting what changes among the options and naming the rule it tests.

slides.title: Grammar II: Agreement, Pronouns, Tense, Confused Words, Capitals, Apostrophes, Commas
slides.board:
Week 8 · Reasoning Through Language Arts

Today you will:

  • Match verbs to their real subjects
  • Choose the right pronoun (I or me, its or their)
  • Keep verb tense steady
  • Tell sound-alike words apart
  • Use capitals, apostrophes, and commas correctly

Plan: Warm-up · Seven rules, each with a quick test · Your turn · GED questions · Recap

notes.say: Last week was about how sentences are built. This week is about the small choices inside a sentence: one letter, one capital, one comma. On the GED, these show up as drop-down menus inside emails, notices, and letters, and the options often differ by a single mark. The good news is that the same few rules come up again and again, and each one has a quick test. By the end of the hour you should be able to look at any menu, name the rule it is testing, and prove your answer.
ask: When you write an email for work, what do you double-check before you hit send? (expected: any honest answer; listen for spelling, names, tone, and build on it: spell-check misses most of what we cover today)

slides.title: Review: last week's sentence skills
slides.board:
Fix each one out loud.

  1. Sentence or fragment? “Because the bus was late again this morning.”
  2. Fix the comma splice: “The printer is jammed, we will use the one upstairs.”
  3. Fix the modifier: “Walking into the lobby, the new carpet caught my eye.”
  4. Make it parallel: “The job requires lifting boxes, to drive a forklift, and inventory counts.”
  5. Pick the transition: “The shop raised prices. (However / Therefore), sales stayed strong.”
steps: 1. Fragment. It starts with Because and never finishes the thought. Fix: “Because the bus was late again this morning, I missed the start of class.”
2. Any of these: “The printer is jammed. We will use…” · “The printer is jammed; we will use…” · “The printer is jammed, so we will use…”
3. “Walking into the lobby, I noticed the new carpet.” The carpet was not walking.
4. “The job requires lifting boxes, driving a forklift, and counting inventory.”
5. However. Higher prices would normally hurt sales; strong sales are a contrast, not a result.

notes.say: This warm-up reviews week 7: fragments, run-ons, modifiers, parallelism, and transitions. Give the student about four minutes for all five, then have them explain each fix before you reveal it. These skills come right back today, because many drop-down menus mix sentence structure with the rules we add this week.
notes.answer: 1. Fragment (dependent clause alone); attach it to a main clause. 2. Period, semicolon, or comma + so. 3. Put the walker right after the comma: “Walking into the lobby, I noticed the new carpet.” 4. lifting, driving, counting. 5. However (contrast).
notes.watch: On number 2, a student may say “add a comma and however.” That is still a comma splice. The fix with however needs a semicolon: “jammed; however, we will…”

slides.title: Spot five
slides.board:
Hi Marcus,

The new schedules is posted in the break room. Please check you're shift for next week, and let me know if their are any problems. Me and Dana will be in the office on monday.

Thanks, Lena

This note has exactly five errors. Find and fix them.
steps: 1. schedules is → schedules are (plural subject, plural verb)
2. you're shift → your shift (belongs to you; “you are shift” makes no sense)
3. their are → there are (introduces something that exists)
4. Me and Dana will be → Dana and I will be (drop “Dana and”: “I will be”)
5. monday → Monday (days of the week are capitalized)

notes.say: This is a preview of today's lesson. Give the student three minutes. Do not teach yet; just see what they notice. Each error matches one of today's rules, so as you reveal them, name the rule and say, “We will learn a quick test for this one.” Point out that a spell-checker would miss almost every one of these.
notes.answer: schedules are · your shift · there are · Dana and I will be · Monday.
notes.watch: If the student finds only two or three, that is normal at this point. Say so, and tell them they will find all five by the end of the hour.

slides.title: Find the real subject
slides.board:
Singular subject → singular verb. Plural subject → plural verb.

SingularPlural
The list isThe lists are
The driver wasThe drivers were
The office hasThe offices have
The nurse worksThe nurses work

Test: cross out the middle. Phrases with of, in, for, with, along with, as well as, including never hold the subject.

There is / There are: the subject comes after the verb.

notes.say: Agreement is the most tested grammar rule on the GED, and the trap is almost always the same: a noun sits right next to the verb, but it is not the subject. Teach the cross-out habit: draw a line through any phrase that starts with a preposition or along with, then match the verb to what is left. Point out the odd thing about the present tense: a singular verb usually has an -s (works), while a plural noun has the -s (nurses). With There is and There are, the word there is never the subject; look after the verb.
ask: In “The keys to the van (is / are) missing,” what do you cross out? (expected: “to the van”; the subject is keys, so are)
In “There (is / are) two messages for you,” what is the subject? (expected: messages, so are)
notes.watch: Students sometimes think an -s on the verb means plural, because an -s on a noun does. Use the table: The nurse works (one) / The nurses work (more than one).

slides.title: Cross out the middle
slides.board:
Choose the verb:

“The list of approved vendors (is / are) posted on the shared drive.”
steps: Step 1. Find the verb choices: is or are.
Step 2. Cross out the phrase: “The list [of approved vendors] (is / are) posted.”
Step 3. What is left? “The list (is / are) posted.” The subject is list: one list.
Step 4. Singular subject → singular verb: “The list of approved vendors is posted on the shared drive.”
Trap: vendors are sounds right because the plural noun is next to the verb.

notes.say: Model the cross-out on the screen: actually draw a line through the phrase. Then show why the wrong answer is tempting: vendors are sounds fine on its own, because vendors is plural and sits right next to the verb. On the GED, the test writers put the plural noun there on purpose.
ask: Try one more: “The cost of the repairs (was / were) higher than expected.” (expected: was; cross out “of the repairs”)

slides.title: Tricky subjects
slides.board:
SubjectVerbExample
each, every, everyone, everybody, someone, nobody, either, neithersingularEveryone on both teams has a badge.
A and BpluralThe cook and the server are here.
A or / nor Bmatch the closer oneNeither the drivers nor the manager was told.
A group as one unit (team, committee, company, family)singularThe committee meets on Tuesdays.

notes.say: These four patterns cover almost every agreement question that is not a cross-out question. Everyone feels like a lot of people, but grammatically it means every one, one at a time, so it takes a singular verb. And adds two subjects together, so the verb is plural. Or and nor do not add; they choose, so the verb matches whichever subject is closer. And a group acting as one unit, like a team or company, is singular in American English.
ask: “Either the tenants or the landlord (pays / pay) for the repair.” Which subject is closer? (expected: landlord, so pays)
“My aunt and my cousin (lives / live) in Tampa.” (expected: live; and makes the subject plural)
notes.watch: Students over-apply the and rule to or/nor and choose a plural verb every time there are two subjects. Have them point to the subject touching the verb.

slides.title: Two subjects with or / nor
slides.board:
Choose the verb:

“Neither the drivers nor the manager (was / were) told about the detour.”
steps: Step 1. Find the subjects: the drivers and the manager.
Step 2. Find the joining word: nor. With or/nor, match the closer subject.
Step 3. The closer subject is the manager, which is singular.
Step 4. “Neither the drivers nor the manager was told about the detour.”
Flip it: “Neither the manager nor the drivers were told.” Now the closer subject is plural.

notes.say: Walk through the joining word first, because it decides which rule applies. With and we would add the subjects; with nor we pick the closer one. Then flip the sentence to show how the answer changes when the order changes. That flip convinces students the rule is about position, not meaning.
ask: Why not “were,” since there are several people? (expected: nor does not add the subjects together; the verb matches the closer subject)

slides.title: Agreement together
slides.board:
Choose the verb. Name the rule each time.

  1. Everyone on the night crews (has / have) a new badge.
  2. The boxes of printer paper in the hallway (needs / need) to be moved.
  3. There (is / are) three messages for you at the front desk.
  4. The committee (meets / meet) on the first Tuesday of each month.
  5. Either the supervisor or the shift leads (signs / sign) the log.
steps: 1. has: Everyone is singular; cross out “on the night crews.”
2. need: cross out “of printer paper in the hallway”; boxes is plural.
3. are: the subject comes after the verb: three messages.
4. meets: the committee acts as one unit.
5. sign: with or, match the closer subject, shift leads (plural).

notes.say: The student answers each one and names the rule before you reveal it. If they name the rule correctly but pick the wrong verb, slow down on the singular/plural verb forms from the earlier table.
notes.watch: On number 2, the nearest noun is hallway (singular), so a student who matches the nearest noun picks needs. Make them cross out both phrases.

slides.title: Pronouns: agreement and case
slides.board:
Subject (does it)Object (gets it)Owner
Imemy, mine
he / shehim / herhis / her, hers
weusour, ours
theythemtheir, theirs
ititits
whowhomwhose

Agree: The company changed its hours. The workers brought their tools.

Test: drop the partner. “Call Jo or (I / me)” → “Call me.”

After between, to, for, with: object form. between you and me

notes.say: Two jobs today. First, a pronoun has to agree with the word it replaces, its antecedent: one company is its, many workers are their. Second, a pronoun changes form depending on its job. If it does the action, use the subject column; if it receives the action or follows a preposition, use the object column. The drop-the-partner test settles almost every case: cover the other person and listen. Mention myself: it is only for when I already appears as the subject (“I fixed it myself”), never as a fancy me. Point to the last row: who works like he (a subject), and whom works like him (an object). Right after a preposition, it is always whom: to whom, both of whom.
ask: “The store changed (its / their) return policy.” (expected: its; one store)
Why is “between you and I” wrong? (expected: between is a preposition, so it takes the object form, me)
“(Who / Whom) left the lights on?” Answer with he or him. (expected: he left them on, so who)
notes.watch: Many adults were taught that “and I” is always more correct. It is correct only when the pronoun is a subject. Drop the partner every time.

slides.title: Drop the partner
slides.board:
Choose the pronouns:

a. “The supervisor asked Tanya and (I / me) to cover the Saturday shift.”

b. “Ms. Reyes can tell you about the work (her and me / she and I) did on the schedule.”
steps: a. Drop the partner: “The supervisor asked (I / me)…” → “asked me.” The pronoun receives the action.
b. Find the verb the pronouns go with: did. Who did the work? They did, so they are subjects.
b. Test each alone: “the work she did” (not “her did”); “the work I did” (not “me did”).
Answers: a. me · b. she and I

notes.say: Do part a first because the test works instantly. Part b is harder because the pronouns come right after about the work, so it feels like they follow a preposition. Show that the pronouns are actually doing the action did, so they are subjects. This is the exact trap the GED likes.
ask: In b, what is the object of the preposition about? (expected: the work, not the pronouns)

slides.title: Pronouns together
slides.board:
Choose the pronoun. Say the test you used.

  1. The bakery announced (its / their) new holiday hours.
  2. Please send the report to Mr. Diaz or (I / me / myself).
  3. Between you and (I / me), the new schedule works better.
  4. Rosa and (she / her) will open the store on Saturday.
  5. Please tell me to (who / whom) I should send the invoice.
steps: 1. its: the antecedent is bakery, one business.
2. me: drop “Mr. Diaz or”: “send the report to me.” Myself needs I as the subject.
3. me: between is a preposition, so object form.
4. she: drop “Rosa and”: “She will open the store.”
5. whom: to is a preposition; answer with he or him: “send it to him,” and whom matches him.

notes.say: Let the student lead. For each one, they say the test (antecedent, drop the partner, or the he/him test for who/whom) and then the answer. Push for the reason on number 2, because myself sounds polite to many people.
notes.watch: If the student picks their for number 1, ask, “How many bakeries?” Businesses and groups acting as one take its.

slides.title: Keep verb tense steady
slides.board:
Time clueTenseExample
yesterday, last year, in 2019, agopastShe called.
now, every day, usuallypresentShe calls.
tomorrow, next week, soonfutureShe will call.
since, for (up to now)present perfectShe has called twice since Monday.

Stay in one tense unless the time really changes.

has/have/had + past participle: has gone, has taken, has written (never has went). Write should have, never should of.

notes.say: Tense questions are clue questions. Before choosing, the student should find the time clue in the sentence or the sentences around it, and look at the other verbs. Shifting tense without a reason is an error. The present perfect is for something that started in the past and continues or matters now, and its signal words are since and for. Note the irregular verbs: after has or have, you need the participle form, so has gone, not has went.
ask: “She (worked / has worked) here since 2019.” Which clue decides it? (expected: since; she still works here, so has worked)
What is wrong with “I should of called”? (expected: it should be should have; “should've” sounds like “should of”)
notes.watch: Students sometimes choose the tense that “sounds” formal (will have been). Always go back to the time clue.

slides.title: Follow the time clues
slides.board:
Choose each verb:

“Last spring, our building (hires / hired) a new manager. On her first day she (walks / walked) every floor and (asks / asked) tenants what needed fixing. Since then, she (was / has been) in charge of every repair in the building.”
steps: Step 1. Time clues: Last spring and On her first day are past; Since then runs from the past up to now.
Step 2. “Last spring, our building hired a new manager.”
Step 3. “She walked every floor and asked tenants…” Joined verbs match, and needed is already past.
Step 4. “Since then, she has been in charge of every repair…” Since then runs from that day up to now, and she is still in charge, so use the present perfect.
Answers: hired · walked · asked · has been

notes.say: Model the routine: underline the time clues first (Last spring, On her first day, Since then), then every verb choice. Show that the paragraph stays in the past until Since then brings it up to now. That one change is a real change in time, so the tense changes with it.
ask: Why is “Since then, she was in charge” wrong? (expected: since then means from that time up to now, and she is still in charge, which calls for has been)

slides.title: Sound-alike words
slides.board:
WordsQuick test
they're · their · therethey are · belongs to them · a place / there is
it's · itsit is or it has · belongs to it
you're · youryou are · belongs to you
who's · whosewho is · belongs to whom
affect · effectto influence (verb) · a result (noun, after a, an, the)
then · thantime, next · comparing
accept · exceptto take · leaving out
to · toodirection, to + verb · also, more than enough

notes.say: Every contraction in this list has the same test: say the long form out loud. If “it is” or “they are” fits, use the apostrophe. If it does not, the word shows ownership or a place, and it has no apostrophe. For affect and effect, look at the word before the blank: after a, an, the, or an adjective, you need the noun, effect. For than, look for a comparison word like more, less, better, or rather.
ask: “The dog wagged (its / it's) tail.” Say the long form. Does it fit? (expected: no, “it is tail” makes no sense, so its)
“The storm had a big (affect / effect).” What word comes before the blank? (expected: big, an adjective after a; so effect, the noun)
notes.watch: The most common error is it's for ownership, because nouns use 's to show ownership. Teach the rule plainly: possessive pronouns (its, hers, ours, yours, theirs, whose) never take an apostrophe.

slides.title: Three sound-alikes in one sentence
slides.board:
Choose each word:

“(Its / It's) clear that the new hours had a big (affect / effect) on sales, which are now higher (then / than) last year's.”
steps: Blank 1. Long form: “It is clear…” makes sense → It's.
Blank 2. The word before is big, an adjective after a, so a noun is needed → effect.
Blank 3. higher is a comparison → than.
Full sentence: “It's clear that the new hours had a big effect on sales, which are now higher than last year's.”

notes.say: Run the test out loud for each blank so the student hears the method, not just the answer. Each blank uses a different test: long form, the word before the blank, and the comparison word.
ask: Make a sentence that uses affect correctly. (expected: any sentence with affect as a verb, such as “Rain can affect the schedule.”)

slides.title: Tense and sound-alikes together
slides.board:
1. Yesterday the mechanic (checks / checked) the brakes and (says / said) they were fine.
  2. Mia (worked / has worked) at the clinic since 2021.
  3. (Whose / Who's) coat is on the chair?
  4. The rain did not (affect / effect) the game.
  5. I should (of / have) called first.
steps: 1. checked, said: Yesterday sets both actions in the past.
2. has worked: since 2021 means she started then and still works there.
3. Whose: “Who is coat” makes no sense; the coat belongs to someone.
4. affect: after did not you need a verb: to influence.
5. have: should have + past participle; should've only sounds like “should of.”

notes.say: The student answers and names the clue or the test for each one. Number 5 is a spelling-by-sound error that is common in casual writing; it shows up in GED menus.
notes.answer: 1. checked, said 2. has worked 3. Whose 4. affect 5. have.
notes.watch: On number 4, students who memorized “affect = verb” sometimes still pick effect because of the word the later in the sentence. Point to the word right before the blank: not.

slides.title: Capitals and apostrophes
slides.board:
Capitalize

  • names of people, places, streets, businesses
  • days, months, holidays
  • languages (Spanish)
  • a title right before a name (Mayor Ellis)

Not: seasons, general words (the mayor, a hospital), most school subjects

Apostrophes

  • one owner: the driver's
  • plural owners ending in -s: the drivers'
  • plural not ending in -s: the children's
  • contractions: don't, it's

Never: plain plurals (two tickets) or its, yours, theirs

notes.say: Capitals have one question: is this the name of one specific person, place, thing, or day? Lincoln Park is a name; the park is not. Seasons are never capitalized in the middle of a sentence, even though months and holidays are. For apostrophes, ask “Does this word own something?” If yes, decide one owner or more than one, then place the apostrophe. If no, there is no apostrophe, unless letters are missing in a contraction.
ask: Capital or not: “We hire extra help every (Summer / summer).” (expected: summer; seasons are not capitalized)
One coach owns the whistle. Two teams own the lockers. Write both. (expected: the coach's whistle; the teams' lockers)
notes.watch: Learners often put an apostrophe on any word ending in -s, including plain plurals and family names (“The Nguyen's live here”). Ask, “What does it own?” If nothing, no apostrophe: The Nguyens.

slides.title: Check every apostrophe and capital
slides.board:
Find and fix three errors:

“The clinic's two nurse's will be off on monday, but it's front desk will stay open.”
steps: Step 1. clinic's: the two nurses belong to (work for) one clinic, so one owner takes 's. Correct.
Step 2. nurse's: the nurses do not own anything here; it is a plain plural → nurses.
Step 3. monday: a day of the week → Monday.
Step 4. it's: “it is front desk” makes no sense; the desk belongs to the clinic → its.
Fixed: “The clinic's two nurses will be off on Monday, but its front desk will stay open.”

notes.say: Model the scan: stop at every apostrophe and every word that could be a name. For each apostrophe, ask “owner or contraction?” For each possible capital, ask “specific name?” One apostrophe here is correct, which is exactly how GED drafts work: not every mark is wrong.
ask: Why does clinic's keep its apostrophe while nurse's loses it? (expected: the clinic owns something; the nurses own nothing in this sentence)

slides.title: Commas: when to use them, when not to
slides.board:
1. After an introductory clause or long phrase: When the meeting ends, lock the door.
  2. Between items in a series: pens, paper, and tape
  3. Before and, but, or, so joining two sentences: The store opened, but the lights were off.
  4. A pair around extra information: Our supervisor, Dana Whitfield, is on site.
  5. (No commas around information that tells which one: The tenant who called is here.)

Never between a subject and its verb. Never between a verb and its object.

notes.say: The rule for commas is simple to say: use one only when you can name the reason. Walk through the four uses, then spend real time on extra information. If the sentence still says which person or thing you mean without the words, they are extra and get a pair of commas. If the words are needed to tell which one, as in “the tenant who called,” they get no commas. When a name comes first and a title follows it (Dana Whitfield, our supervisor,), the title is always extra, because the name already tells who. Finally, the two don'ts: a single comma between a subject and its verb is always wrong, and so is one between a verb and its object.
ask: “Our landlord Ms. Patel fixed the heater.” There is only one landlord. Where do commas go? (expected: after landlord and after Patel)
“Workers who finish early may leave.” Commas or not? (expected: none; who finish early tells which workers)
notes.watch: Students who add a comma at every pause will over-punctuate. Ask them to name the rule for each comma they add. No rule, no comma.

slides.title: A menu where only commas change
slides.board:
“[ ▾ ] the store will close early on Friday.”

A. Because the floors are being refinished,
B. Because the floors are being refinished
C. Because, the floors are being refinished,
D. Because the floors, are being refinished,
steps: Step 1. The words are the same in every option, so this is a comma question.
Step 2. “Because the floors are being refinished” is an introductory clause (subject floors, verb are being refinished). It needs a comma after it, so B is wrong.
Step 3. C puts a comma right after Because, splitting the clause from its first word. Wrong.
Step 4. D puts a comma between the subject floors and its verb are being refinished. Wrong.
Answer: A. “Because the floors are being refinished, the store will close early on Friday.”

notes.say: This is exactly how the GED tests commas: the words are identical and only the commas move. Model the first move, which is noticing that only the commas change. Then name the rule and test each option.
ask: How did you know this was a comma question before reading closely? (expected: the words were the same in every option)

slides.title: Edit a notice together
slides.board:
Notice to Tenants: Parking Lot Repaving

The parking lot, along with both side driveways, (1) [is / are] closed this Friday. Last year, repaving took two days and (2) [causes / caused / will cause] very few problems. (3) [Their / There / They're] will be free parking on Oak Avenue all day. (4) [If it rains, the / If it rains the / If, it rains the] work will move to Monday. Tenants who need help moving a car should call Ms. Cho or (5) [I / me / myself].
steps: (1) is: cross out “along with both side driveways”; the subject is lot.
(2) caused: Last year and took set the time in the past.
(3) There: it introduces something that exists; “They are will be” makes no sense.
(4) If it rains, the: comma after the introductory clause, none after If.
(5) me: drop “Ms. Cho or”: “call me.”

notes.say: This is a mixed set, the way the GED mixes rules in one document. For every choice, the student names the rule first, then the answer. Do not confirm an answer until the rule is named.
notes.answer: (1) is (2) caused (3) There (4) If it rains, the (5) me.
notes.watch: On (5), myself is the popular wrong answer. Myself works only when I is the subject of the same sentence.

slides.title: Your turn: agreement and pronouns
slides.board:
3 minutes. Choose the correct word.

  1. The cost of the new uniforms (is / are) higher this year.
  2. Neither the cashiers nor the manager (knows / know) the new code.
  3. The trainer showed Malik and (I / me) the new software.
  4. The team won (its / their) third game in a row.
steps: 1. is (subject: cost)
2. knows (closer subject: manager)
3. me (showed me)
4. its (one team)

notes.say: Start a three-minute timer and stay quiet while the student works. When time is up, have them give each answer with the rule before you reveal anything.
notes.answer: 1. is: cross out “of the new uniforms.” 2. knows: with nor, match the closer subject, manager. 3. me: drop “Malik and”: “showed me.” 4. its: the team acts as one unit.
notes.watch: A student who answers know on number 2 is adding the subjects. Ask which word is touching the verb.

slides.title: Your turn: tense, sound-alikes, capitals
slides.board:
4 minutes.

  1. Last week I (call / called) the office and (ask / asked) for a refund.
  2. (Your / You're) going to need (your / you're) ID at the door.
  3. Fix the capitals: “we visited aunt rosa in chicago last summer.”
steps: 1. called, asked
2. You're, your
3. “We visited Aunt Rosa in Chicago last summer.” (summer stays lowercase)

notes.say: Start a four-minute timer. On number 3, the student should say which words change and which stay lowercase, and why.
notes.answer: 1. called, asked: Last week is past, and joined verbs match. 2. You're (you are going), your (the ID belongs to you). 3. We (first word), Aunt Rosa (title used with a name, and the name), Chicago (city); summer stays lowercase because seasons are not capitalized.
notes.watch: If the student leaves aunt lowercase, explain that a family title used as part of a name is capitalized (Aunt Rosa), but not after my (my aunt).

slides.title: Your turn: apostrophes and commas
slides.board:
4 minutes.

  1. All forty workers use the (employee's / employees') lounge.
  2. Add the comma: “When the alarm sounds leave through the side door.”
  3. Add the commas: “Our landlord Ms. Patel fixed the heater.” (There is only one landlord.)
  4. Fix it: “We need volunteer's for Saturday.”
steps: 1. employees'
2. “When the alarm sounds, leave through the side door.”
3. “Our landlord, Ms. Patel, fixed the heater.”
4. “We need volunteers for Saturday.”

notes.say: Start a four-minute timer. For each comma the student adds, they must name the rule.
notes.answer: 1. employees': plural owners ending in -s take only an apostrophe. 2. A comma after the introductory clause. 3. A pair of commas around extra information that renames the one landlord. 4. volunteers: a plain plural, no apostrophe.
notes.watch: On number 3, a single comma after Patel splits the subject from its verb. Extra information takes a pair.

slides.title: GED question: agreement
slides.board:
Starting today, the new hours for the pool, along with the updated fee schedule, [ ▾ ] posted at the front desk.

A. is
B. are
C. were
D. being
steps: A is wrong: is agrees with fee schedule, but that noun is inside the “along with” phrase, which never holds the subject.
C is wrong: were is plural but past tense, and “Starting today” sets the time in the present.
D is wrong: being cannot be the main verb; the sentence would have no verb.
B is correct: cross out “for the pool” and “along with the updated fee schedule”; the subject hours is plural and the time is now: “the new hours… are posted.”

notes.say: Treat this like the real test. Have the student say what changes among the options first (the verb), then find the real subject before looking at the options. Then eliminate together, naming the reason each time.
ask: What two phrases do you cross out? (expected: for the pool; along with the updated fee schedule)
notes.answer: B. are. The subject is hours (plural); “Starting today” calls for the present tense.

slides.title: GED question: extra information
slides.board:
From an email to Northside Clinic staff:

[ ▾ ] will lead the new-hire training on Friday.

A. Gloria Banks, our office manager,
B. Gloria Banks, our office manager
C. Gloria Banks our office manager,
D. Gloria, Banks, our office manager,
steps: B is wrong: it opens the extra information with a comma but never closes it, so “our office manager” runs into the verb will lead.
C is wrong: the title has no comma before it, so the only comma falls between the subject and its verb will lead.
D is wrong: a comma inside her name splits Gloria from Banks; no rule calls for it.
A is correct: the name already tells exactly who will lead the training, so “our office manager” is extra information, set off by a pair of commas.

notes.say: The name comes first, so it already tells exactly who will lead the training. The title after it adds extra information. Have the student cover “our office manager” and check: do we still know who? Then eliminate, naming the reason each time.
ask: Cover “our office manager.” Do we still know who will lead the training? (expected: yes, Gloria Banks; so the title is extra and takes a pair of commas)
notes.answer: A. Gloria Banks, our office manager, will lead the new-hire training on Friday.

slides.title: GED strategy: spot the difference first
slides.board:
1. Compare the options. What exactly changes?
  2. Name the rule. A verb changes → agreement or tense. One letter or word → sound-alikes or pronouns. A capital → name or not? A comma moves → comma rules.
  3. Test with the quick test: cross out, drop the partner, say the long form, find the time clue.
  4. Read the whole sentence with your choice in place.

Editing menus are quick points. Aim for under a minute each and save time for the long reading passages.

notes.say: The worst way to answer a drop-down is to ask “Which one sounds right?” Many wrong answers sound right, because they match how people talk. Comparing the options first tells you which rule is being tested, and then the quick test proves the answer. This is also faster, which matters: editing questions should take less than a minute each, so the student banks time for the longer reading questions in the same part of the test.
ask: If the options are “its / it's / its',” what rule is being tested and what is the test? (expected: sound-alike or apostrophe; say “it is” and see if it fits)

slides.title: Recap and next steps
slides.board:
• Agreement: cross out the middle; each/everyone singular; or/nor → closer subject.
  • Pronouns: match the antecedent; drop the partner; between you and me; who = he, whom = him.
  • Tense: follow the time clue; since → has/have.
  • Sound-alikes: say the long form.
  • Capitals, apostrophes, commas: name the rule or leave it out.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice Set A (Set B if under 80%) → Exit Check

notes.say: Before revealing the recap, have the student name the quick test for each rule from memory: cross out the middle, drop the partner, find the time clue, say the long form, and name the comma rule. Then walk through what comes next: the Student Lesson reviews each rule with checks, Practice Set A has 15 GED-style editing questions with the reasoning behind every wrong answer, and the Exit Check confirms they are ready for week 9, when we start the extended response.
ask: Which rule from today do you most need to practice? (expected: any honest answer; point them to that screen in the Student Lesson)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, you will read short drafts such as emails, notices, and letters. Some sentences contain drop-down menus, and you choose the version that is correct. The choices often differ by one letter, one capital, or one comma. The same few rules come up over and over, and each one has a quick test. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • make verbs agree with their real subjects
  • choose pronouns that agree and use the right case (I or me)
  • keep verb tense consistent with the time clues
  • tell sound-alike words apart (its/it's, their/there/they're, affect/effect, than/then)
  • use capital letters, apostrophes, and commas correctly

Work one screen at a time. Most screens end with a check question that you must answer before moving on. If you miss it, you will see exactly why that answer is wrong.

screens.title: Find the real subject
screens.html:
A verb must agree with its subject. A singular subject (one) takes a singular verb; a plural subject (more than one) takes a plural verb.

SingularPlural
The manager signsThe managers sign
The box is / was / hasThe boxes are / were / have

Notice that in the present tense, the singular verb usually ends in -s, while the plural noun ends in -s.

Test: cross out the middle. Phrases that start with of, in, on, for, with, along with, as well as, or including never contain the subject. Cross them out, then match the verb to what is left.

example.prompt: “The cost of the new uniforms (is / are) higher than last year.”
steps: Cross out “of the new uniforms.”
What is left: “The cost (is / are) higher.” The subject is cost, which is singular.
A singular subject takes a singular verb.
example.answer: “The cost of the new uniforms is higher than last year.” Uniforms are sounds natural only because uniforms sits next to the verb.

check.prompt:
“The box of old files in the supply closet (is / are) too heavy to lift.”

Type the correct verb: is or are.
check.hint: Cross out every phrase that starts with of or in. What noun is left?
check.explain: Cross out the two phrases: “The box [of old files] [in the supply closet] (is / are) too heavy.” The subject is box, which is singular, so the verb is is. The plural files is the trap; it is inside a phrase that starts with of.

mistakes.why: You matched the verb to files or closet. Cross out “of old files” and “in the supply closet.” The subject is box, one box, so the verb is is.

screens.title: When the subject comes after the verb
screens.html:
In most sentences the subject comes first. In a few patterns, it comes after the verb, so you have to look ahead.

  • There is / There are / There was / There were: There is never the subject. There are two problems. There is one problem.
  • Here is / Here are: Here are the keys.
  • Questions: Where are the new forms?

Test: turn it around. “There (is / are) three messages” → “Three messages (is / are) there.” Now the subject is up front: messages are.

example.prompt: “There (was / were) several complaints about the noise last night.”
steps: Turn it around: “Several complaints (was / were) there.”
The subject is complaints, which is plural.
The time clue last night keeps it in the past.
example.answer: “There were several complaints about the noise last night.”

check.prompt:
Which verb correctly completes the sentence?

“There ____ several good reasons to arrive ten minutes early on test day.”
check.hint: There is never the subject. Look after the blank.
check.explain: Turn the sentence around: “Several good reasons (are) there.” The subject is reasons, which is plural, so the verb is are. Is is tempting because “There is” is such a common phrase, but there is never the subject.
why: You treated There as the subject. The real subject comes after the verb: reasons, which is plural.
Was is singular, and it is past tense. The subject reasons is plural, and the sentence gives advice for now.
Has been is a singular form. The subject reasons is plural, so it would need have been.

screens.title: Tricky subjects: each, everyone, and, or, nor
screens.html:
SubjectVerbExample
each, every, everyone, everybody, someone, nobodysingularEach of the tablets has a case.
A and BpluralThe nurse and the doctor are in.
A or / nor Bmatch the closer subjectNeither the cooks nor the manager was told.
a group acting as one (team, committee, company, family)singularThe committee meets monthly.

Everyone feels like many people, but it means every one, one at a time, so it is singular. And adds subjects together. Or and nor choose between them, so the verb matches the subject touching it.

example.prompt: “Either the tenants or the landlord (pays / pay) for the repair.”
steps: The joining word is or, so match the closer subject.
The closer subject is the landlord, which is singular.
example.answer: “Either the tenants or the landlord pays for the repair.” If you flip it, “Either the landlord or the tenants pay.”

check.prompt:
Choose the correct verb for each sentence.

“Everyone in both evening classes {{0}} a locker key.”

“Neither the drivers nor the dispatcher {{1}} the new route yet.”
check.hint: Everyone means every one. For nor, find the subject touching the verb.
check.explain:
Sentence 1: Everyone is singular. Cross out “in both evening classes” and you get “Everyone has a locker key.”

Sentence 2: With neither… nor, match the subject closer to the verb. That is the dispatcher, so “Neither the drivers nor the dispatcher knows the new route yet.” The plural know is tempting because there are several people, but nor does not add subjects.

why: Have is plural. Everyone is singular, and “in both evening classes” is a phrase that does not change the subject.
Having cannot be the main verb of a sentence; the sentence would have no real verb.
You added the two subjects together, which works with and. With nor, the verb matches the closer subject, the dispatcher, which is singular.
Are knowing is plural, and know is not normally used in the -ing form for a state of mind. The closer subject is singular: knows.

screens.title: Pronouns must match what they replace
screens.html:
A pronoun stands in for a noun. The noun it replaces is its antecedent. A pronoun must match its antecedent in number.

  • The employees picked up their checks. (many employees → their)
  • The company changed its policy. (one company → its)
  • The residents must move their cars. (not his or her, which is singular)

Test: find the antecedent. Ask, “Whose? Who?” Point to the noun, decide one or many, and choose the pronoun that matches. A business, store, school, or team acting as one is it, so it takes its.

example.prompt: “The clinic will extend (its / their) hours, and the nurses will take (its / their) lunch breaks in shifts.”
steps: Blank 1: whose hours? The clinic's. One clinic → its.
Blank 2: whose lunch breaks? The nurses'. Many nurses → their.
example.answer: “The clinic will extend its hours, and the nurses will take their lunch breaks in shifts.”

check.prompt:
Choose the pronoun that agrees with its antecedent.

“The hospital updated {{0}} visiting hours, and the volunteers signed {{1}} names on the new schedule.”
check.hint: For each blank, ask whose? and point to the noun.
check.explain: Blank 1: whose visiting hours? The hospital's. One hospital → its. Blank 2: whose names? The volunteers'. Many volunteers → their.

why: Their is plural. The antecedent is the hospital, one institution, so it takes its.
It's means “it is.” “Updated it is visiting hours” makes no sense; the possessive is its.
Its would point back to the hospital, but the names belong to the volunteers, who are plural.
His or her is singular. The antecedent volunteers is plural, so it takes their.

screens.title: Pronoun case: drop the partner
screens.html:
Pronouns change form depending on their job in the sentence.

Subject (does the action)Object (receives the action or follows to, for, with, between)
I, he, she, we, they, whome, him, her, us, them, whom

Mistakes happen when a pronoun is paired with another person. “Me and Dana went” and “He called Dana and I” both sound normal in speech, but both are wrong in writing.

Test: drop the partner. Cover the other person and read the sentence with only the pronoun. “Ms. Bell called Jo and (I / me)” → “Ms. Bell called me.”

example.prompt: “My sister and (I / me) start classes in January.”
steps: Cover “My sister and.”
Read both: “I start classes” or “Me start classes.”
The pronoun does the action start, so it is a subject.
example.answer: “My sister and I start classes in January.”

check.prompt:
“The manager gave Jordan and ____ the keys to the storage room.”

Type the correct pronoun: I or me.
check.hint: Cover “Jordan and” and read the sentence with each pronoun.
check.explain: Drop “Jordan and”: “The manager gave me the keys.” The pronoun receives the action, so it takes the object form. “And I” sounds polite, which is why it is tempting, but it is correct only for subjects.

mistakes.why: Drop the partner: “The manager gave I the keys” does not work. The pronoun receives the keys, so it takes the object form, me.
Myself is used only when I is already the subject (“I locked it myself”). Here the manager is the subject, so use me.

screens.title: More pronoun traps: between, myself, who and whom
screens.html:
• Between, to, for, with, from are prepositions. The pronouns after them take the object form: between you and me, for her and me.
  • Myself is not a polite me. Use it only when I is already the subject: I fixed it myself. Wrong: Call Ana or myself.
  • Who / whom: who matches he (a subject); whom matches him (an object). (Who / Whom) called? → He called → Who. To (who / whom) should I send it? → to him → whom. Right after a preposition, always use whom: to whom, for whom, both of whom.

When a pronoun follows a preposition, you can still drop the partner: “for Ana and (I / me)” → “for me.”

example.prompt: “Between you and (I / me), the old schedule worked better.”
steps: Between is a preposition.
Pronouns after a preposition take the object form.
example.answer: “Between you and me, the old schedule worked better.”

check.hint: Drop the partner in each sentence and listen.
check.explain: Drop the partner in each sentence. “Please call me with any questions” is correct because the pronoun receives the action. “Call myself” is the most tempting wrong answer because it sounds formal, but myself works only when I is the subject. “Ms. Ortiz and me will answer” uses the object form for a subject.
options: Please call Ms. Ortiz or me with any questions.
Please call Ms. Ortiz or myself with any questions.
Please call Ms. Ortiz or I with any questions.
Ms. Ortiz and me will answer your questions.
why: Myself needs I as the subject of the same sentence. Here the reader is being asked to call, so use the object form, me.
Drop the partner: “Please call I” does not work. The pronoun receives the call, so it must be me.
Drop the partner: “Me will answer” does not work. The pronoun does the action, so it must be the subject form: “Ms. Ortiz and I will answer.”

screens.title: Keep verb tense consistent
screens.html:
Tense tells when an action happens. Before you choose a verb, find the time clue and look at the other verbs nearby.

Time cluesTenseExample
yesterday, last week, in 2019, agopastI called the office.
now, every day, usuallypresentI call the office.
tomorrow, next monthfutureI will call the office.

Stay in the same tense unless the time really changes. Shifting for no reason is an error:

  • Wrong: Last week I called the office and ask for a refund.
  • Right: Last week I called the office and asked for a refund.

Verbs joined by and usually share the same tense.

example.prompt: “Yesterday I (call / called) the landlord, and he (fixes / fixed) the sink an hour later.”
steps: Time clue: Yesterday, which is past.
Both actions happened yesterday, so both verbs are past.
example.answer: “Yesterday I called the landlord, and he fixed the sink an hour later.”

check.prompt:
Choose the verbs that keep the tense consistent.

“Last October, the crew {{0}} the old roof in two days and {{1}} new shingles by Friday.”
check.hint: Find the time clue at the start of the sentence.
check.explain: The time clue “Last October” sets the paragraph in the past, and both actions are finished. Use the simple past for both: the crew tore off the old roof and installed new shingles.

why: Tears off is present tense, but “Last October” places the work in the past.
Will tear off is future tense, but “Last October” places the work in the past.
Installs is present tense. It is joined by and to a past action in a past time frame, so it should be past too.
Has installed does not fit a finished action at a specific past time (“Last October… by Friday”). Use the simple past.

screens.title: Since, for, and verbs with has and have
screens.html:
Use the present perfect (has or have + past participle) for an action that started in the past and continues now or still matters now. The signal words are since and for.

  • She has worked here since 2019. (she still works here)
  • We have lived in this city for six years.

Many common verbs are irregular. After has, have, or had, use the third form:

TodayYesterdayhas / have / had…
gowentgone
taketooktaken
writewrotewritten
seesawseen
beginbeganbegun

Also: write should have, could have, would have, never should of.

example.prompt: “Since March, the bridge on Route 9 (was / has been) closed for repairs.”
steps: Since March means from March up to now, and the bridge is still closed.
That calls for has + past participle: has been.
example.answer: “Since March, the bridge on Route 9 has been closed for repairs.”

check.prompt:
Which word correctly completes the sentence?

“Marcus has already ____ three letters to the city about the pothole on his street.”
check.hint: What form follows has? Think write, wrote, ____.
check.explain: After has, use the past participle. For write, the forms are write, wrote, written, so the answer is has written. Wrote is the most tempting wrong answer because it is past tense, but “has wrote” mixes two forms, like “has went.”
why: Wrote is the simple past form. After has, you need the past participle: has written.
Writes is present tense and cannot follow has. Has + past participle: has written.
Has writing is not a verb form in English. After has, use the past participle written.

screens.title: Sound-alike words: the contraction test
screens.html:
Some words sound the same but do different jobs. Most of them are a contraction and a possessive.

Contraction (has an apostrophe)Possessive or other (no apostrophe)
it's = it is / it hasits = belonging to it
they're = they aretheir = belonging to them · there = a place, or “there is”
you're = you areyour = belonging to you
who's = who iswhose = belonging to whom

Test: say the long form. Replace the word with “it is,” “they are,” “you are,” or “who is.” If the sentence still makes sense, use the contraction. If not, use the word without an apostrophe.

example.prompt: “(Its / It's) time to check (your / you're) email.”
steps: Blank 1: “It is time” makes sense → It's.
Blank 2: “check you are email” makes no sense → your.

check.prompt: Click the sentence that uses a sound-alike word incorrectly.
check.hint: Replace each sound-alike with its long form: it is, they are, you are.
check.explain: Say the long form for each word. “It is open all night” makes sense, so the sentence needs it's, not its. The other words are correct: Their shows ownership, “It is about a ten-minute walk” fits It's, There is introduces something that exists, and “You are welcome” fits You're.
spans: Their new apartment is on the third floor.
It's about a ten-minute walk from the bus stop.
The building has a laundry room, and its open all night.
There is a small park across the street.
You're welcome to visit any weekend.
check.why: The most common miss is the sentence with Their. Say the long form: “They are new apartment” makes no sense, so their (belonging to them) is correct there. The error is “its open all night,” which means “it is open.”

screens.title: Sound-alike words: meaning pairs
screens.html:
WordsMeaningExample
affect / effectto influence (a verb) / a result (a noun)Rain can affect turnout. The rain had an effect.
then / thantime or next step / comparingWe ate, then left. Taller than his brother.
accept / exceptto take or agree / leaving outWe accept cards. Open daily except Sunday.
to / too / twodirection, or before a verb / also, more than enough / 2too hot; two keys; go to work
lose / looseto misplace / not tightDon't lose the loose screw.

Clues: After a, an, the, or an adjective, use the noun effect. After more, less, better, rather, use than.

example.prompt: “The new hours had a big (affect / effect) on sales, which are higher (then / than) last year.”
steps: Blank 1 follows a big, so it needs a noun: effect.
Blank 2 follows higher, a comparison: than.
example.answer: “The new hours had a big effect on sales, which are higher than last year.”

check.prompt:
Choose the correct word for each blank.

“The storm had no {{0}} on the race.”

“This year's crowd was bigger {{1}} last year's.”

“The store will {{2}} returns for thirty days.”
check.hint: Look at the word right before each blank.
check.explain: 1. After “had no,” the sentence needs a noun meaning result: effect. 2. Bigger is a comparison: than. 3. The store will take returns: accept.

why: Affect is usually a verb. After “had no,” you need a noun meaning “result”: effect.
Affects is a verb form. After “had no,” you need a noun: effect.
Then tells time or a next step. Bigger is a comparison, so use than.
“Bigger that last year's” is not standard English. Comparisons use than.
Except means “leaving out.” The store is agreeing to take returns, so use accept.
Expect means “to look forward to” or “to predict,” which does not fit a store's return policy. The meaning is “take”: accept.

screens.title: Capital letters
screens.html:
Capitalize the first word of a sentence and the names of specific people, places, and things (proper nouns).

Capitalize

  • people: Dana Whitfield
  • places and streets: Chicago, Juniper Street, Lincoln Park
  • businesses and groups: Bayside Foods
  • days, months, holidays: Monday, March, Labor Day
  • languages: English, Spanish
  • a title right before a name: Mayor Ellis, Aunt Rosa

Do not capitalize

  • seasons: spring, fall
  • general words: the street, a park, the mayor, my aunt
  • most school subjects: math, history

Test: Is this the name of one specific person, place, thing, or day? Lincoln Park is a name. the park is not.

example.prompt: “next fall, my sister will take spanish at riverside community college.”
steps: First word: Next.
spanish is a language: Spanish. The college is a specific name: Riverside Community College.
fall is a season and stays lowercase; sister is a general word.
example.answer: “Next fall, my sister will take Spanish at Riverside Community College.”

check.prompt:
“This spring, my cousin will take english and math classes at the college on monday nights.”

Select two words that should be capitalized.
check.hint: Which words name one specific language or day?
check.explain: English is a language, and languages are always capitalized. Monday is a day of the week. Spring is a season, math is a school subject that is not a language, and cousin and the college are general words, so they stay lowercase.
why: Seasons are not capitalized in the middle of a sentence.
Cousin is a general word here. It would be capitalized only as a title right before a name, as in “Cousin Lena.”
Most school subjects are not capitalized. Only languages, such as English, are.
“The college” is a general reference, not the college's full name.

screens.title: Apostrophes that show ownership
screens.html:
An apostrophe can show that something belongs to someone. Where it goes depends on how many owners there are.

OwnerRuleExample
one owneradd 'sthe driver's license
more than one owner, word ends in -sadd only 'the drivers' lounge
more than one owner, word does not end in -sadd 'sthe children's room, the women's team

Test: say “belonging to.” Write the owner word first, decide whether it is one or many, then add the apostrophe. “The lounge belonging to the drivers” → drivers → drivers'.

example.prompt: “I planned the (cashier's / cashiers') schedules for all twelve cashiers.”
steps: Who owns the schedules? The cashiers, and there are twelve.
Plural owner ending in -s: add only an apostrophe.
example.answer: “I planned the cashiers' schedules for all twelve cashiers.”

check.prompt: The lockers belong to all of the nurses on the floor. Type the possessive word that completes the phrase: “the ____ lockers.”
check.hint: First write the owner word in its plural form. Then decide where the apostrophe goes.
check.explain: Start with the owner: nurses (many). The word ends in -s, so add only an apostrophe: the nurses' lockers.

mistakes.why: Nurse's means one nurse owns the lockers. There are many nurses, and the plural nurses already ends in -s, so add only an apostrophe: nurses'.
Nurses is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it does not show ownership. Add an apostrophe after the -s: nurses'.
A plural that already ends in -s does not take another -s. Add only the apostrophe: nurses'.

screens.title: Contractions, and where apostrophes never go
screens.html:
An apostrophe also marks missing letters in a contraction: do not → don't, it is → it's, they are → they're, we will → we'll.

Apostrophes never go in these places:

  • Plain plurals: three tickets, not three ticket's. The Nguyens live next door, not The Nguyen's.
  • Possessive pronouns: its, his, hers, ours, yours, theirs, whose already show ownership.
  • Plain verbs: She runs, not She run's.

Test: For every apostrophe, ask two questions. Are letters missing? Does this word own the next word? If both answers are no, remove the apostrophe.

example.prompt: “We baked three batches of cookie's for the Nguyen's party.”
steps: cookie's: do the cookies own anything? No. It is a plural → cookies.
Nguyen's: the party belongs to the Nguyen family, more than one person → Nguyens'.
example.answer: “We baked three batches of cookies for the Nguyens' party.”

check.prompt: Click the sentence that has an apostrophe error.
check.hint: For each apostrophe, ask: missing letters, or an owner?
check.explain: In “three batches of muffin's,” the muffins do not own anything. It is a plain plural, so it should be muffins. The other sentences are correct: Nguyens is a plain plural, kids' shows plural owners, its is a possessive pronoun, and They're means “they are.”
spans: The Nguyens moved in next door last week.
Their kids' bikes are already in the yard.
Their dog wags its tail at everyone.
We baked three batches of muffin's to welcome them.
They're planning a cookout for Saturday.
check.why: The sentence with kids' bikes is the most common wrong click. The bikes belong to more than one kid, and kids ends in -s, so the apostrophe after the -s is correct.

screens.title: Commas: introductions, lists, and joined sentences
screens.html:
Use a comma only when you can name the rule. Here are three of the rules:

  1. After an introductory clause or long phrase. When the meeting ends, please lock the door. Because the floors are wet, use the side entrance.
  2. Between items in a series of three or more. We ordered pens, paper, and tape. (Some styles leave out the last comma before and, but including it is always correct.)
  3. Before and, but, or, so when they join two complete sentences. The store opened at nine, but the lights were still off. If the second part is not a complete sentence, no comma: The store opened at nine but stayed dark.

Do not put a comma right after because, when, if, or and. The comma goes at the end of the introductory part or before the joining word.

example.prompt: Add commas: “after the meeting on Tuesday we ordered paper pens and folders.”
steps: Capitalize the first word. “After the meeting on Tuesday” is an introductory phrase: comma after Tuesday.
Three items in a series: commas after paper and pens.
example.answer: “After the meeting on Tuesday, we ordered paper, pens, and folders.”

check.hint: Find where the introductory clause ends. Then count the items in the list.
check.explain: The correct sentence has a comma after the introductory clause (“After the meeting ended,”) and commas between the three items in the series (cleaned, stacked, locked). The version with “and, locked” is tempting because it has the same number of commas, but they are in the wrong places.
options: After the meeting ended, we cleaned the room, stacked the chairs, and locked the door.
After the meeting ended we cleaned the room, stacked the chairs, and, locked the door.
After the meeting ended, we cleaned the room stacked the chairs and locked the door.
After the meeting, ended we cleaned the room, stacked the chairs, and locked the door.
why: This leaves out the comma after the introductory clause and adds a comma after and, which separates and from the item it introduces.
The introductory comma is right, but the series of three actions has no commas between the items.
The comma is in the middle of the introductory clause. It splits the subject meeting from its verb ended. It belongs after ended.

screens.title: Commas around extra information
screens.html:
When words add extra information that could be removed without losing track of who or what you mean, set them off with a pair of commas.

  • Our supervisor, Dana Whitfield, will be on site. (We have one supervisor; the name is extra.)
  • Dana Whitfield, our supervisor, will be on site. (The name already tells who; the title is extra.)
  • My car, which is twelve years old, still runs well.

When the words tell which one, they are needed, so use no commas:

  • The tenant who called last night is here. (Which tenant? The one who called.)
  • Anyone who wants a ride should meet at the door.

screens.title: The drop-down routine
screens.html:
On the GED, each drop-down menu tests one rule. Before you choose, compare the options and find exactly what changes. That tells you which rule to use.

What changesThinkQuick test
the verb (is/are, called/calls)agreement or tensecross out the middle; find the time clue
a pronoun (I/me, its/their)pronoun case or agreementdrop the partner; find the antecedent
a sound-alike (their/there)confused wordssay the long form
a capital or an apostrophecapitals or apostrophesspecific name? owner or missing letters?
only commas movecomma rulesname the rule or leave it out

Then read the whole sentence with your choice in place before moving on.

check.prompt: Each set of options below comes from a GED-style menu. Drag each one to the rule it is testing.
check.hint: For each set, ask: what is the only thing that changes?
check.explain: is / are / were: the verb changes, so it is agreement or tense. their / there / they're: sound-alikes. Thanksgiving / thanksgiving: a capital letter changes. cashier's / cashiers' / cashiers: only the apostrophe moves. The last set has the same words with the commas in different places: comma rules.
choices: If it rains, the / If it rains the / If, it rains the
check.why: The most common mistake is putting “cashier's / cashiers' / cashiers” with sound-alike words. The words are the same; only the apostrophe moves, so it tests apostrophes (who owns, and how many owners).

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
Here are the rules to carry into Practice:

  • Agreement: cross out phrases in the middle. Each, every, everyone are singular. And makes a plural. With or/nor, match the closer subject. With There is/are, the subject comes after the verb.
  • Pronouns: match the antecedent (company → its, workers → their). Drop the partner to choose I/me, she/her. Use object forms after prepositions: between you and me. Who works like he; whom works like him (always whom right after a preposition).
  • Tense: follow the time clues; do not shift without a reason. Since and for call for has/have + past participle (has written).
  • Sound-alikes: say the long form; effect after a/the; than for comparisons.
  • Capitals: specific names, days, months, holidays, languages; not seasons or general words.
  • Apostrophes: owners and contractions only; never plain plurals or its, yours, theirs.
  • Commas: after introductions, in a series, before and/but/so joining two sentences, a pair around extra information; never between a subject and its verb.

Next: Practice Set A (15 questions). Score 80% or higher on first tries to master it; otherwise take Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 1 of the email.

“The tablets sends each patient's information directly to our scheduling system, so we will no longer need to type it in by hand.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined word?
items.hint: Find the subject of the verb. Is it one tablet or more than one?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the subject: The tablets. It ends in -s and the email says there are two tablets, so the subject is plural.

Step 2. A plural subject needs a plural verb. In the present tense, the plural form has no -s: The tablets send.

Step 3. Check the tense. The rest of the email describes how the system will work from now on in the present and future (“we will no longer need”), so present tense fits.

Why the others are wrong: sends, is sending, and has sent are all singular forms (they go with it or the tablet), so none of them agrees with tablets. Has sent would also wrongly suggest an action already completed.
why: Sends is the singular form; it goes with one tablet. The subject The tablets is plural (the email says there are two), so the verb is send.
Is sending is singular (it goes with it or the tablet), and it describes something happening at this moment instead of how the system works.
Has sent is singular and describes something already finished. The subject is plural, and the sentence describes how the tablets will work from now on.

items.prompt:
Read the email. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): “Patients will still need to show {{0}} insurance cards to the receptionist, who will scan them as usual.”

Paragraph 2, blank (B): “Please wipe down each tablet and {{1}} case after every patient, using the gray cloths in the top drawer rather than spray cleaner.”
items.hint: Try replacing each choice with its long form: “they are” or “it is.” If the long form makes no sense, it is not the contraction.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The cards belong to the patients, so the word must show ownership. Step 2: Test they're: “show they are insurance cards” makes no sense. Step 3: There points to a place or begins “there is/are”; it does not show ownership. Step 4: Their means “belonging to them.” Answer: their insurance cards.

Blank (B). Step 1: The case belongs to the tablet, so the word must show ownership. Step 2: Test it's: “each tablet and it is case” makes no sense, so it's is wrong. Step 3: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe, and its' is not a word. Answer: its case.

why: There points to a place or begins “there is/are.” The cards belong to the patients, so you need the possessive their.
They're means “they are.” “Show they are insurance cards” makes no sense, so use the possessive their.
It's means “it is.” “Each tablet and it is case” makes no sense; the case belongs to the tablet, so use its.
Its' is not a word. Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: its.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 3 of the email.

“Check-in took about four minutes less per patient then it did with paper forms, and the staff there reported fewer mistakes in phone numbers and addresses.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined word?
items.hint: Is the sentence telling when something happened, or comparing two things?
items.explain:
Step 1. Decide what the sentence is doing. It compares the time check-in takes with tablets to the time it took with paper forms.

Step 2. Comparisons use than, especially after words like less, more, fewer, and rather: “four minutes less per patient than it did with paper forms.”

Why the others are wrong: Then refers to time or a next step (“first this, then that”), so it does not make a comparison. That and as do not complete a comparison that begins with less; “less ... as” and “less ... that it did” are not standard English.
why: Then refers to time or a next step (“first this, then that”). The sentence compares tablets with paper forms after the word less, so it needs than.
“Less… that it did” is not standard English. A comparison that begins with less is completed with than.
As completes comparisons of sameness (“as fast as”). After less, the comparison word is than.

Step 2. Two subjects joined by and make a plural subject.

Step 3. A plural subject in the present tense takes the verb without -s: “The receptionist and the nurse on duty share responsibility.” Shares is tempting because nurse, the noun closest to the verb, is singular, but the and joins two people.

Shared changes the tense to the past. The email describes how things will work starting Monday, so the verb stays in the present: share.
Sharing cannot be the main verb of a sentence; “The receptionist and the nurse sharing responsibility” is a fragment. Use share.

Read the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 1, blank (A): “The town will replace the water main under {{0}} between Elm Avenue and Fourth Street.”

Paragraph 1, blank (B): “Crews will begin work the week after Labor Day, and the project should be complete by late {{1}}.”

Blank (B). Step 1: Check each word. Step 2: Seasons (fall, spring, summer, winter) are general words and are not capitalized, so “Fall” is wrong in the middle of a sentence. Step 3: Holidays are proper nouns and are capitalized, like “Labor Day” earlier in the sentence. Answer: fall, before Thanksgiving. why: Juniper Street is the name of one specific street, so both words are capitalized, just like Elm Avenue and Fourth Street in the same sentence.
Street is part of the street's name here, so it is capitalized too, as in Fourth Street.
Juniper is part of the proper name and must be capitalized. Both words of a street name take capitals.
Seasons are not capitalized in the middle of a sentence, so Fall should be lowercase.
Holidays are proper nouns and are capitalized, like Labor Day earlier in the sentence: Thanksgiving.
This reverses both rules: the season should be lowercase and the holiday should be capitalized.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 2 of the notice.

“Residents who park on the street should move his or her vehicles to the lot behind Larkspur Elementary School before 7:00 a.m. on weekdays.”

items.hint: Which word does the pronoun refer back to? Is that word singular or plural?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the antecedent, the word the pronoun refers to. The vehicles belong to the Residents.

Step 2. Residents is plural, so the pronoun must be plural: their.

Step 3. Check spelling: the possessive form is their (belonging to them). Answer: “Residents ... should move their vehicles.”

Why the others are wrong: His or her is singular, so it does not match a plural antecedent. Its is singular and refers to things, not people. There is a place word, not a possessive, so it is a confused-word error.
why: His or her is singular. The pronoun refers to Residents, which is plural, so it must be their.
Its is singular and refers to things, not people. The vehicles belong to the residents, so use their.
There is a place word, not a possessive. The vehicles belong to the residents: their.

items.prompt:
Read the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 3, blank (C): “{{0}} please fill several containers with drinking water the night before.”

Paragraph 3, blank (D): “During the work, you may also notice {{1}}”

Blank (C). Step 1: “Because water service to each home will be off for up to six hours” is an introductory clause: it has a subject (water service) and a verb (will be), and it comes before the main part of the sentence (please fill ...). Step 2: An introductory clause is followed by a comma, so the option with no comma is wrong. Step 3: No comma belongs right after Because, and no comma belongs between the subject water service to each home and its verb will be. Answer: the version with a single comma after hours, at the end of the clause.

Blank (D). Step 1: The list has three items: noise, dust, and short traffic delays. Step 2: Items in a series of three or more are separated by commas, with and before the last item: “noise, dust, and short traffic delays.” Step 3: The other options either leave out the commas entirely or put a comma after and, which wrongly separates and from the item it introduces. Because water service to each home will be off for up to six hours

Because water service to each home, will be off for up to six hours,

A comma right after Because splits the clause from the word that introduces it. No rule calls for it.
This comma falls between the subject water service to each home and its verb will be. Never separate a subject from its verb.

options: noise, dust, and short traffic delays.
noise dust and short traffic delays.
noise, dust and, short traffic delays.
noise, dust, and, short traffic delays.
why: Three items in a series need commas between them. Without commas, the list runs together.
