items.prompt: Read paragraph 2 of the newsletter article. Click the sentence that contains an error in the use of an apostrophe.
items.hint: For each apostrophe, ask whether the word owns the next word or whether letters are missing. If neither, it should not be there.
items.explain:
Step 1. Check every apostrophe and ask, “owner or missing letters?”

  • garden's: the beds belong to one garden. Correct.
  • bed's: the renter of each bed. Correct.
  • gardeners': the shed belongs to many gardeners. Correct.
  • store's: the stores do not own anything in this sentence; the writer means two stores. Error.
  • children's: children is a plural that does not end in -s, so it takes 's. Correct.
  • It's: “It is the most popular spot.” Correct.

Step 2. The sentence should read “Two local hardware stores donated the shed and most of the tools.”
spans: The garden's forty beds are rented for $15 a season.
Each bed's renter agrees to water and weed at least twice a week.
The gardeners' tool shed holds shovels, hoses, and wheelbarrows that anyone may borrow.
Two local hardware store's donated the shed and most of the tools.
The children's corner has four small beds where kids from the after-school program grow pumpkins.
It's the most popular spot in the garden every October.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence with gardeners', because the apostrophe comes after the -s. That is the correct form for many owners: the shed belongs to all the gardeners. The real error is store's, which is only a plural.

items.prompt:
Read paragraph 1 of the newsletter article. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Blank (A): “Last April, a group of neighbors {{0}} a vacant lot on Ferris Street into the Northgate Community Garden.”

Blank (B): “Volunteers hauled away twelve truckloads of trash and {{1}} forty raised beds in a single weekend.”

Blank (C): “Since that first spring, the garden {{2}} more than two tons of vegetables to the Northgate Food Pantry.”
items.hint: Find the time clue in each sentence. Which one runs from the past up to now?
items.explain:
Blank (A). The time clue “Last April” is a finished past time, so use the simple past: turned.

Blank (B). This verb is joined by and to hauled, and both happened in “a single weekend” in the past: built.

Blank (C). The clue changes: Since that first spring runs from the past up to now. That calls for the present perfect, and the singular subject the garden takes has: the garden has donated more than two tons. Donates is tempting because the article is about the present, but it describes a habit, not a total built up since that first spring.

why: Turns is present tense, but “Last April” places the action in the past.
Will turn is future tense, but “Last April” places the action in the past.
Builds is present tense. It is joined by and to the past-tense hauled, and both actions happened in one past weekend.
Will build is future tense, but the beds were built in the same past weekend that volunteers hauled away the trash.
Have donated is the plural form. The subject the garden is singular, so it takes has donated.
Donates describes a regular present habit. The clue Since that first spring totals up what has happened from then until now, which calls for has donated.
Will donate looks ahead, but the sentence counts what the garden has already given since last spring.

items.prompt: Read these sentences from paragraph 3 of the newsletter article. Select two sentences that contain an error in subject-verb agreement.
items.hint: For each sentence, cross out the phrases in the middle and match the verb to what is left.
items.explain:
The committee… meet is an error. Cross out “that runs the garden”: “The committee meet.” A committee acting as one group is singular, so it should be meets.

Each of the beds have is an error. Cross out “of the beds”: “Each have.” Each is singular, so it should be has. The plural beds right before the verb is the trap.

The other three sentences are correct: Every gardener receives, Gardeners must bring… the garden provides, and The Northgate Food Pantry picks.
options: Every gardener receives a key to the main gate.
Gardeners must bring their own seeds, but the garden provides compost and mulch.
The committee that runs the garden meet on the first Monday of each month.
Each of the beds have a small sign with the renter's name.
The Northgate Food Pantry picks up extra vegetables every Friday.
why: Every gardener is singular, and receives is singular. This sentence is correct.
Gardeners must bring and the garden provides both agree: plural with plural, singular with singular.
The pantry is one organization, and picks is singular. This sentence is correct.

items.prompt:
Read paragraphs 3 and 5 of the newsletter article. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 3: “When we started, the older gardeners taught {{0}} everything we know about soil,” says Luz Ferreira.

Paragraph 5, blank (I): “Questions about the workshop can go to Sam Okafor, {{1}} keeps the sign-up sheet.”

why: Both pronouns are in the subject form. They receive the teaching (the older gardeners taught them), so both need the object form: him and me.
Him is right, but I is not. Drop the partner: “the older gardeners taught I” does not work. Use me.
Me is right, but he is not. Drop the partner: “the older gardeners taught he” does not work. Use him.
Whom is the object form, like him. Here the word does the action keeps: “he keeps the sign-up sheet,” so use who.
Which refers to things, not people. Sam Okafor is a person, so use who.
Whose shows ownership, as in “whose sheet.” Here the word does the action keeps, so use the subject form who.

items.hint: For the first blank, test each pronoun alone after taught. For the second, answer with he or him: does he keep the sheet, or does him?
items.explain:
Paragraph 3. Step 1: The subject of taught is the older gardeners. The pronouns are the people being taught, so they receive the action. Step 2: Pronouns that receive an action take the object form: me, him, her, us, them. Step 3: Drop the partner to check each one: “taught him everything” and “taught me everything.” Answer: him and me. The trap is “him and I,” which sounds formal; “and I” is correct only for subjects.

Blank (I). Step 1: Find the verb that goes with the blank: keeps. Step 2: Answer with he or him: “he keeps the sign-up sheet,” not “him keeps.” He is a subject, and who matches he. Answer: “Sam Okafor, who keeps the sign-up sheet.” Whom is tempting because it sounds formal, but it is the object form, like him.

items.prompt:
Read paragraph 4 of the newsletter article. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Blank (D): “{{0}} hard to believe that the garden is only one year old.”

Blank (E): “Ask any of the {{1}} families what they like best, and you will hear about friendships, not just food.”

Blank (F): “Some gardeners worry that the new fence on the north side will {{2}} how much sunlight the back beds receive.”
items.hint: For (D), try “It is.” For (E), count the owners. For (F), look at the word right before the blank.
items.explain:
Blank (D). Read it as “It is hard to believe.” That makes sense, so use the contraction It's.

Blank (E). The families belong to the gardeners, and there are many gardeners (forty beds). For a plural owner ending in -s, add only an apostrophe: gardeners'.

Blank (F). After the helping verb will, you need a verb in its base form. The verb meaning “to influence” is affect. Effect is the most tempting wrong answer, but it is a noun, as in “a big effect.”

why: Its shows ownership. Read the long form: “It is hard to believe” makes sense, so you need the contraction It's.
Its' is not a word in English. The sentence means “It is hard to believe”: It's.
Gardener's means one gardener owns the families. The garden has many gardeners, so the owner is plural: gardeners'.
Gardeners has no apostrophe, so it does not show that the families belong to the gardeners.
A plural that already ends in -s takes only an apostrophe, not another -s.
Effect is usually a noun meaning “result.” After will, you need a verb meaning “to influence”: affect.
Affects has the wrong form after will. The helping verb will is followed by the base form: will affect.
Effects is a plural noun. After will, you need the verb affect.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 3 of the newsletter article.

“The list of rules for new gardeners, along with the watering schedule, are posted on the shed door.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined word?
items.hint: Cross out every phrase between the subject and the verb, including the one that starts with along with.
items.explain:
Step 1. Cross out the phrases in the middle: “The list [of rules] [for new gardeners], [along with the watering schedule], (is / are) posted.”

Step 2. What is left is “The list (is / are) posted.” The subject is list, which is singular.

Step 3. The paragraph is in the present tense (receives, provides, picks up), so use the singular present: “The list… is posted on the shed door.”

Why are is tempting: two plural nouns sit before the verb, and “along with” seems to add a second item. But a phrase that begins with along with never changes the subject; only and does.
why: Are is plural. It agrees with rules or gardeners, or treats “along with the watering schedule” as adding a second subject. The subject is list.
Were is plural and past tense. The subject list is singular, and the rules are posted now.
Have been is a plural form. The singular subject list would need has been, and the simple present is fits the rest of the paragraph.

items.prompt:
Read paragraph 5 of the newsletter article. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Blank (G): “{{0}} will hold a free workshop on composting on Saturday, May 9.”

Blank (H): “{{1}} must sign up at the shed by Thursday.”
items.hint: For each blank, cover the words that describe the person or people. Do you still know exactly who is meant?
items.explain:
Blank (G). The name Rosa Delgado already tells exactly who will hold the workshop, so the title after it is extra information: remove it and we still know who. Extra information takes a pair of commas: “Rosa Delgado, our neighborhood association president, will hold….”

Blank (H). “Who wants a seat” tells which people must sign up. Without it, the sentence would say that anyone at all must sign up. Information that tells which one is essential and takes no commas: “Anyone who wants a seat must sign up.” The version with a pair of commas is tempting because it looks like blank (G), but the two clauses do different jobs.

options: Rosa Delgado, our neighborhood association president,
Rosa Delgado, our neighborhood association president
Rosa Delgado our neighborhood association president,
Rosa, Delgado, our neighborhood association president,
why: This opens the extra information with a comma but never closes it, so the title runs into the verb will hold. Extra information takes a pair of commas.
The title is extra information, so it needs a comma before it too. With only one comma, that comma falls between the subject and its verb, will hold.
A comma inside a person's name splits Rosa from Delgado; no rule calls for it.
The commas mark “who wants a seat” as extra information, but it is needed: it tells which people must sign up. Information that tells which one takes no commas.
This comma falls between the whole subject, “Anyone who wants a seat,” and its verb, must sign up. Never separate a subject from its verb.
This comma cuts “who wants a seat” off from Anyone, even though the clause is needed to tell which people must sign up.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 4 of the newsletter article.

“Last summer, mayor Ellis visited the garden and praised the volunteer's for there hard work.”

Which revision of the sentence corrects all of its errors?
items.hint: Check every capital letter, every apostrophe, and every sound-alike word. A correct revision must fix all of them and break nothing.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the errors in the original. mayor is a title right before a name, so it is capitalized: Mayor Ellis. volunteer's is a plain plural (the volunteers do not own anything), so no apostrophe: volunteers. there is a place word; the hard work belongs to the volunteers, so it should be their.

Step 2. Check what is already right: summer is a season and stays lowercase.

Step 3. Only one revision fixes all three errors without adding a new one: “Last summer, Mayor Ellis visited the garden and praised the volunteers for their hard work.” The revision with volunteers' is the most tempting, but moving the apostrophe does not fix a plain plural.
options: Last summer, Mayor Ellis visited the garden and praised the volunteers for their hard work.
Last Summer, Mayor Ellis visited the garden and praised the volunteers for their hard work.
Last summer, Mayor Ellis visited the garden and praised the volunteers' for their hard work.
Last summer, mayor Ellis visited the garden and praised the volunteers for they're hard work.
why: This fixes the title, the plural, and their, but it capitalizes Summer. Seasons are not capitalized.
This moves the apostrophe instead of removing it. The volunteers do not own anything here; it is a plain plural: volunteers.
This leaves mayor lowercase before the name, and they're means “they are,” which makes no sense before “hard work.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 1 of the letter.

“In fact, the skills in your list of requirements matches the work I do every day.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined word?
items.hint: Cross out the phrase that starts with in. Is what is left one thing or more than one?
items.explain:
Step 1. Cross out the phrase: “the skills [in your list of requirements] (matches / match) the work.”

Step 2. The subject is skills, which is plural.

Step 3. A plural subject takes the present-tense verb with no -s: “the skills in your list of requirements match the work I do every day.” Matches is the trap: the singular list sits right before the verb.
why: Matches is singular. It agrees with list, the noun right before the verb, but list is inside the phrase “in your list of requirements.” The subject is skills.
Is matching is singular, and the subject skills is plural. The plural form would be are matching, but the simple present match fits a general fact.
Has matched is singular and describes a finished action. The subject skills is plural, and the sentence states a fact about now.

items.prompt:
Read paragraph 1 of the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

“If {{0}} on the morning shift, {{1}} will be a short training in the break room each day at 7:15 a.m.”
items.hint: Replace each choice with its long form: you are, they are. Which ones still make sense?
items.explain:
Blank 1. Say the long form: “If you are on the morning shift” makes sense, so use you're.

Blank 2. The word introduces something that exists, as in “there is” or “there will be.” Use there. Their is tempting because it is the most common spelling, but nothing belongs to anyone here.

why: Your shows ownership. “If your on the morning shift” has no verb; the sentence means “If you are,” so use you're.
You were puts the condition in the past, but the rest of the sentence (will be) is about next month. The meaning is “If you are”: you're.
Their shows that something belongs to a group. Here the word introduces something that exists (“there will be a training”), so use there.
They're means “they are.” “They are will be a short training” makes no sense.

items.prompt:
Read paragraph 1 of the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

“Each training will be shorter {{0}} last year's safety meeting, and it will start at a time that is not {{1}} early for workers coming off the night shift.”
items.hint: Is the first blank comparing or telling time? Does the second blank mean also or more than enough?
items.explain:
Blank 1. Shorter compares this year's training with last year's meeting, so use than.

Blank 2. The meaning is “more than it should be”: not too early. To is the tempting wrong answer because it is the most common of the three spellings.

why: Then tells time or a next step. After the comparison word shorter, use than.
“Shorter that last year's” is not standard English. Comparisons use than.
To shows direction or goes before a verb (“to work”). The meaning here is “more than is good”: too early.
Two is the number 2, which makes no sense before early.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 1 of the newsletter article.

“A retired electrician and a high school student runs the lamp table each month, and they can fix almost any cord or switch.”

Type the correct form of the underlined verb.
items.hint: How many people run the lamp table? Look at the word that joins them.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the subject: A retired electrician and a high school student.

Step 2. Two subjects joined by and are plural. The second half of the sentence confirms it: they can fix.

Step 3. A plural subject in the present tense takes the verb with no -s: they run the lamp table. Runs is tempting because student, right before the verb, is singular.

mistakes.why: Runs is singular. The subject is two people joined by and, an electrician and a student, so the subject is plural and the verb is run. The sentence even refers back to them as they.
Ran changes the tense to the past. “Each month” and “they can fix” describe something that happens regularly now, so keep the present: run.
Running cannot be the main verb of a sentence. Use the present-tense verb run.

items.prompt:
Read paragraph 2 of the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Blank (E): “If you are hurt on the job, report the injury to {{0}} right away, even if it seems minor.”

Blank (F): “A second round of forklift training will be held early next year in {{1}}.”
items.hint: Only the capital letters change. Ask of each word: is it the name of one specific month, holiday, or person?
items.explain:
Blank (E). A title such as shift supervisor is capitalized only when it comes right before a name, as in “Supervisor Ortiz.” After the, it is a general word: the shift supervisor.

Blank (F). Months and holidays are proper nouns: January, after New Year's Day. After stays lowercase because it is not part of a name.

why: A job title is capitalized only when it comes right before a person's name (Supervisor Ortiz). Used alone after the, it is a general word.
Supervisor is not part of a name here, so it stays lowercase. Capitalizing only one word of the title makes it no more correct.
The blank is in the middle of a sentence, so the should not be capitalized.
Months are proper nouns and are always capitalized: January.
Holidays are proper nouns, so every main word of the name is capitalized: New Year's Day.
After is an ordinary word in the middle of the sentence and should be lowercase.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 3 of the memo.

“The company will also update their safety manual this spring.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined word?
items.hint: Whose manual is it? Is that noun singular or plural?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the antecedent: whose safety manual? The company's.

Step 2. A company acting as one unit is singular, so the pronoun is singular: its.

Step 3. Check the spelling: the possessive its never takes an apostrophe. Answer: “The company will also update its safety manual.” Their is tempting because a company is made of many people, but the word company itself is singular.
why: Their is plural. The antecedent is The company, one business acting as a unit, so the pronoun must be singular: its.
It's means “it is.” “Update it is safety manual” makes no sense; the possessive pronoun its has no apostrophe.
There is a place word, not a possessive. The manual belongs to the company: its.

items.prompt:
Read paragraph 3 of the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Blank (G): {{0}}

Blank (H): “Each worker will receive {{1}}”
items.hint: For (G), is each side of but a complete sentence? For (H), how many items are in the list?
items.explain:
Blank (G). “The loading dock will close at 2:00 p.m. on Friday” and “the front office will stay open until 6:00” are both complete sentences. When and, but, or, or so joins two complete sentences, a comma goes before the joining word, not after it.

Blank (H). The list has three items: a hard hat, safety glasses, and steel-toe boots. Commas separate the items, with and before the last one: “a hard hat, safety glasses, and steel-toe boots.” The versions with a comma after and are the common traps.

options: The loading dock will close at 2:00 p.m. on Friday, but the front office will stay open until 6:00.
The loading dock will close at 2:00 p.m. on Friday but the front office will stay open until 6:00.
The loading dock will close at 2:00 p.m. on Friday, but, the front office will stay open until 6:00.
The loading dock will close, at 2:00 p.m. on Friday but the front office will stay open until 6:00.
why: Two complete sentences joined by but need a comma before but. Without it, the two ideas run together.
The comma after but separates the joining word from the sentence it introduces. The comma goes only before but.
This comma splits the verb will close from the time that completes it, and the comma that belongs before but is missing.

options: a hard hat, safety glasses, and steel-toe boots.
a hard hat safety glasses and steel-toe boots.
a hard hat, safety glasses, and, steel-toe boots.
a hard hat, safety glasses and, steel-toe boots.
why: Three items in a series need commas between them. Without commas, “hard hat safety glasses” reads like one item.
The comma after and separates and from the last item. The commas go between the items, before and.
The comma after and is in the wrong place; it belongs before and, after glasses.

items.prompt: Read paragraph 2 of the newsletter article. Click the sentence that contains an error in the use of an apostrophe.
items.hint: For each apostrophe, ask: is this word showing ownership or a contraction? If it is only a plural, it should not have an apostrophe.
items.explain:
Step 1. Check every apostrophe in the paragraph.

  • center's back room: the back room belongs to one center. Correct.
  • Last month's total: the total belongs to last month. Correct.
  • visitors' questions: the questions belong to many visitors, so the apostrophe goes after the -s. Correct.
  • volunteer's who can sew: nothing belongs to the volunteers here. The writer simply means more than one volunteer. Error.

Step 2. The sentence “We are always looking for volunteer's who can sew” uses an apostrophe to make a plural. It should read “We are always looking for volunteers who can sew.”

Step 3. The remaining sentences have no apostrophes and no errors. A common trap is choosing “visitors' questions” because the apostrophe comes after the -s, but that is the correct form for a plural owner.
spans: The Repair Café meets on the second Saturday of every month in the community center's back room.
Volunteers fix lamps, toasters, bicycles, and clothing at no charge.
Last month's total was a record: forty-one items repaired.
The volunteers answer visitors' questions as they work, so many people learn to make simple repairs themselves.
We are always looking for volunteer's who can sew.
If you can thread a needle, we can teach you the rest.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence with visitors' questions, because the apostrophe comes after the -s. That is the correct form when many visitors own the questions. The error is volunteer's, a plain plural.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 2 of the letter.

“Last year, I trained six new cashiers and create a checklist that cut our opening time by fifteen minutes.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined word?
items.hint: Look at the time clue at the start of the sentence and at the other verbs in it.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the time clue: “Last year” places the action in the past.

Step 2. Look at the other verbs. Trained and cut are both past tense, and create is joined to trained by and, so the two verbs should match.

Step 3. The past tense of create is created: “I trained six new cashiers and created a checklist.”

Why the others are wrong: Create and am creating are present tense, and will create is future tense. All three shift away from the past for no reason, which is a tense-consistency error.
why: Create is present tense. “Last year” and the past-tense trained place the action in the past, and verbs joined by and should match.
Will create is future tense, but the sentence describes something that already happened “Last year.”
Am creating describes something happening right now, but the time clue “Last year” places the action in the past.

items.prompt: Read paragraph 4 of the memo. Select two sentences that contain an error in subject-verb agreement.
items.hint: For each sentence, cross out the phrases in the middle and match the verb to what is left.
items.explain:
The boxes… has been moved is an error. Cross out “of cleaning supplies in aisle 6”: “The boxes has been moved.” Boxes is plural, so it should be have been moved. The singular aisle 6 right before the verb is the trap.

The safety committee review is an error. A committee acting as one group is singular, so it should be reviews.

The other sentences are correct: Every forklift driver needs, Both the day crew and the night crew will attend, and Nobody… is allowed.
options: Every forklift driver needs a new certification card by April 1.
The boxes of cleaning supplies in aisle 6 has been moved to aisle 9.
Both the day crew and the night crew will attend the fire drill.
The safety committee review every accident report within a week.
Nobody on the loading dock is allowed to wear headphones.
why: Every forklift driver is singular, and needs is singular. This sentence is correct.
Will attend is the same for singular and plural subjects, and the two crews joined by and make a plural subject. This sentence is correct.
Nobody is singular, and is is singular; “on the loading dock” does not change the subject. This sentence is correct.

items.prompt:
Read paragraphs 3 and 4 of the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 3: “My store manager, Ms. Reyes, has offered to speak with you about the work {{0}} did together on the holiday schedule.”

Paragraph 4, blank (D): “I have also included two references, both of {{1}} worked with me at Bayside Foods.”

why: Both pronouns are in the object form. They are the ones who did the work, so they are subjects and need she and I.
I is right, but her is not. Drop the partner: “the work her did” does not work. Use she.
She is right, but me is not. Drop the partner: “the work me did” does not work. Use I.
Who is the subject form, like he or they. The word comes right after the preposition of, so it takes the object form: “both of them” → whom.
Which refers to things, not people. The references are people, so use whom.
Whose shows ownership, but nothing follows it for the references to own. After the preposition of, use the object form whom.

items.hint: For the first blank, test each pronoun alone with did. For the second, look at the word right before the blank: is it a preposition?
items.explain:
Paragraph 3. Step 1: In the clause “(that) ___ and ___ did together,” the pronouns are the ones doing the action did, so they are subjects. Step 2: Subjects take subject case: I, he, she, we, they. Step 3: Drop the partner to check: “the work she did” (not “her did”) and “the work I did” (not “me did”). Answer: she and I. The trap is that the clause comes right after the preposition about, but the object of about is the work, not the pronouns.

Blank (D). Step 1: The word right before the blank is of, a preposition. Step 2: A pronoun after a preposition takes the object form. Test it: “both of them,” not “both of they.” Whom is the object form, like him and them. Answer: “both of whom worked with me.” Who is tempting because it is more common in speech, but right after a preposition, use whom.

items.prompt:
Read the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 1, blank (A): “{{0}} clear from your job posting that you need someone who can train new staff and keep a busy store running smoothly.”

Paragraph 2, blank (B): “I also planned the {{1}} schedules for the holiday season, making sure that all twelve cashiers had at least one weekend day off.”

Paragraph 3, blank (C): “Good scheduling had a positive {{2}} on our team.”
items.hint: For (A), try “It is.” For (B), count the owners: how many cashiers have schedules? For (C), look at the word “a” before the blank.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: Read it as “It is clear from your job posting.” That makes sense, so the contraction It's is correct. Step 2: Its shows possession (“Its clear” would mean “the clear belonging to it”), and Its' is not a word. Answer: It's.

Blank (B). Step 1: The schedules belong to the cashiers, so a possessive is needed. Step 2: The sentence says there are twelve cashiers, so the owner is plural. Step 3: For a plural noun ending in -s, add only an apostrophe: cashiers'. Step 4: Cashier's means one cashier; cashiers has no apostrophe to show ownership; cashiers's adds an extra -s that plural possessives do not take.

Blank (C). Step 1: The blank follows “a positive,” so it must be a noun (a thing), and a singular one because of a. Step 2: Effect is the noun meaning “result.” Answer: “a positive effect on our team.” Step 3: Affect and affects are verbs, and effects is plural, which does not fit after a.

why: Its shows ownership. Read the long form: “It is clear from your job posting” makes sense, so use the contraction It's.
Its' is not a word in English. The sentence means “It is clear”: It's.
Cashier's means one cashier. The letter says all twelve cashiers had schedules, so the owner is plural: cashiers'.
Cashiers has no apostrophe, so it does not show that the schedules belong to the cashiers.
A plural that already ends in -s takes only an apostrophe, not another -s.
Affect is usually a verb. After “a positive,” you need a noun meaning “result”: effect.
Affects is a verb form. After “a positive,” you need a singular noun: effect.
Effects is plural, which does not fit after a. Use the singular effect.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 3 of the newsletter article.

“Neither the organizers nor the center's director expect the event to make money.”

Which is the correct way to write the underlined word?
items.hint: When two subjects are joined by “neither ... nor,” the verb agrees with the subject that is closer to it.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the subjects: the organizers and the center's director, joined by neither ... nor.

Step 2. With or or nor, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. The closer subject is the center's director, which is singular.

Step 3. The paragraph is in the present tense (“does not charge,” “The goal is”), so use the singular present form: “Neither the organizers nor the center's director expects the event to make money.”

Why the others are wrong: Expect, are expecting, and have expected are all plural forms. They would agree with organizers, but that subject is farther from the verb. Treating two subjects as automatically plural works with and, not with nor.
why: Expect is plural. It would agree with organizers, but with neither… nor the verb matches the closer subject, the center's director, which is singular.
Are expecting is plural. With nor, the verb agrees with the closer subject, the center's director, which is singular.
Have expected is plural and shifts away from the paragraph's simple present (“does not charge,” “The goal is”). The closer subject is singular: expects.

items.prompt:
Read paragraph 5 of the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Blank (I): “{{0}} will lead Friday's fire drill.”

Blank (J): “{{1}} should see me before Friday.”
items.hint: For each blank, cover the words that describe the person or people. Do you still know exactly who is meant?
items.explain:
Blank (I). The name Teresa Gomez already tells exactly who will lead the drill, so the title after it is extra information: remove it and we still know who. Extra information takes a pair of commas: “Teresa Gomez, our safety director, will lead….”

Blank (J). “Who cannot attend the drill” tells which workers should see the manager. Without it, the sentence would tell every worker to come in. Information that tells which one takes no commas: “Any worker who cannot attend the drill should see me before Friday.” The version with a pair of commas is tempting because it matches blank (I), but the two parts do different jobs.

why: This opens the extra information with a comma but never closes it, so the title runs into the verb will lead. Extra information takes a pair of commas.
The title is extra information, so it needs a comma before it too. With only one comma, that comma falls between the subject and its verb, will lead.
A comma inside a person's name splits Teresa from Gomez; no rule calls for it.

options: Any worker who cannot attend the drill
Any worker, who cannot attend the drill,
Any worker who cannot attend the drill,
Any worker, who cannot attend the drill
why: The commas mark “who cannot attend the drill” as extra information, but it is needed: it tells which workers should see the manager. Information that tells which one takes no commas.
This comma falls between the whole subject, “Any worker who cannot attend the drill,” and its verb, should see. Never separate a subject from its verb.
This comma cuts “who cannot attend the drill” off from Any worker, even though the clause is needed to tell which workers should see the manager.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 4 of the newsletter article.

“On saturday, march 14, the Repair Café will hold it's first spring event at Lincoln Park.”

Which revision of the sentence corrects all of its errors?
items.hint: Check each word that could be capitalized: is it a specific name, day, or month, or is it a season or general word? Then test “it's” by reading it as “it is.”
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the errors in the original. saturday is a day of the week and march is a month, so both must be capitalized. It's means “it is,” and “will hold it is first spring event” makes no sense, so the possessive its is needed.

Step 2. Check the words that are already correct. spring is a season, so it stays lowercase. Lincoln Park is the name of a specific park, so both words stay capitalized. Repair Café is the name of the group, so it stays capitalized.

Step 3. Only one revision fixes all three errors and keeps every correct word: “On Saturday, March 14, the Repair Café will hold its first spring event at Lincoln Park.”

Why the others are wrong: One revision keeps it's and wrongly capitalizes Spring. Another leaves saturday lowercase and lowercases park in a proper name. The remaining one capitalizes Spring and lowercases park.
options: On Saturday, March 14, the Repair Café will hold its first spring event at Lincoln Park.
On Saturday, March 14, the Repair Café will hold it's first Spring event at Lincoln Park.
On saturday, March 14, the Repair Café will hold its first spring event at Lincoln park.
On Saturday, March 14, the Repair Café will hold its first Spring event at Lincoln park.
why: This keeps it's, which means “it is,” and it capitalizes the season Spring. Seasons are not capitalized.
This fixes its and March but leaves saturday lowercase, and it lowercases Park, which is part of the park's name.
This capitalizes the season Spring and lowercases Park in the proper name Lincoln Park.

stimuli.title: Draft Email: Volunteer Orientation at the Eastside Food Bank
stimuli.source: Original document written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
The following email is a first draft. Lettered blanks mark places where you will choose the correct option. Some other sentences contain errors that the questions ask about.

To: New Volunteers

vocab.def: The word or words that tell who or what a sentence is about; the doer of the action.
The rule that a singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb.
A group of words that begins with a word such as of, in, on, with, or for. It never contains the subject of the sentence.
A pronoun that does not name a specific person or thing, such as each, everyone, someone, or nobody. Most are singular.
The word a pronoun replaces or refers to.
vocab.example: The company changed its hours. (company is the antecedent of its)

vocab.def: The form a pronoun takes depending on its job: subject case (I, she, we) or object case (me, her, us).
The form of a verb that shows when an action happens: past, present, or future.
A verb form made with has or have plus a past participle, used for an action that began in the past and continues or still matters now.
Words that sound alike but have different spellings and meanings.
A shortened word in which an apostrophe replaces missing letters.
vocab.example: it's = it is; they're = they are

vocab.def: A form that shows ownership, usually with an apostrophe for nouns. Possessive pronouns (its, theirs, yours) never use one.
The name of a specific person, place, organization, or thing. It is always capitalized.
A word, phrase, or clause that comes before the main part of a sentence. It is usually followed by a comma.
Extra information that can be removed without changing the basic meaning of the sentence. It is set off with a pair of commas.
vocab.example: Our supervisor, Dana Whitfield, is on site.

vocab.def: The verb form used after has, have, or had. For regular verbs it ends in -ed; many common verbs are irregular.

notes:
Week 8 RLA Study Sheet: Grammar II

Subject-verb agreement

  • Cross out phrases in the middle (of, in, with, along with, as well as).
  • each, every, everyone, nobody, someone = singular
  • A and B = plural
  • A or/nor B = match the closer one
  • There is (one) / There are (many): subject comes after the verb
  • A company, team, or committee = singular

Pronouns

SubjectObject
I, he, she, we, they, whome, him, her, us, them, whom
  • Drop the partner: Jo and (I/me)
  • between you and me
  • who = he (subject); whom = him (object): to whom, both of whom
  • Plural antecedent → their; a thing → its

Verb tense

  • Follow time clues; do not switch without a reason.
  • has/have + participle: past that continues now (since, for).
  • has gone, has written, has taken; should have, never should of

Confused words

WordMeans
they're / it's / you'rethey are / it is / you are
their / its / yourbelongs to
thereplace; there is/are
affect / effectto influence / a result
than / thencompare / time
accept / excepttake / leave out
who's / whosewho is / belongs to whom

Capitals

YES: names, streets, cities, days, months, holidays, languages, title + name. NO: seasons, general words, most school subjects.

Apostrophes

  • one owner: 's; plural owners ending in -s: s'
  • contractions: don't, it's
  • NEVER for plain plurals or its, yours, theirs

Commas

  • after an introductory element
  • items in a series (3+)
  • before and/but/or/so joining two sentences
  • a pair around extra information (none if it tells which one)
  • NEVER between subject and verb

Drop-down routine: (1) Spot what changes among the options. (2) Name the rule. (3) Read the whole sentence with each option. (4) Choose.
